Cargo: the one tool Rust is compiled : rustc , the compiler, turns source files into a machine-code program before anything runs.
You rarely call it yourself.
Cargo is the build tool and package manager: it creates projects, downloads dependencies, calls rustc , runs tests and lints.
A package of Rust code is a crate ; the public registry is crates.io .
Toolchains are installed and updated by rustup (here the stable 1.99.0 of 2026-10-01; a new stable ships every six weeks, RELEASES.md ).
Correction to the old page The old "Rust: zero to expert" page gave stable 1.98 (2026-08-20) as current; 1.99.0 was released on 2026-10-01 and is what every example here ran on.

Its claim that Edition 2024 is current still holds: cargo new on 1.99.0 writes edition = "2024" , below. $ cargo new hello && cd hello && find . -not -path "./.git/*" -not -name .git | sort && cat Cargo.toml && cat src/main.rs Creating binary (application) `hello` package note: see more `Cargo.toml` keys and their definitions at https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html . ./.gitignore ./Cargo.toml ./src ./src/main.rs [package] name = "hello" version = "0.1.0" edition = "2024" [dependencies] fn main() { println!("Hello, world!"); } Cargo.toml plays the role of pyproject.toml . edition = "2024" picks the language edition : editions let Rust make small incompatible changes every few years while crates of different editions still link together (2024 has been stable since 1.85.0, Edition Guide ). cargo run compiles and runs: $ cargo run Compiling hello v0.1.0 (hello) Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in <time> Running `target/debug/hello` Hello, world! " dev profile, unoptimized + debuginfo" is a debug build: fast to compile, slow to run, with extra checks (section 3).
Always measure with cargo run --release , which turns the optimiser on; section 11 measures what the optimiser does to a loop.

The commands you will use daily Command What it does Python equivalent cargo new name new project (add --lib for a library) uv init cargo add serde add a dependency to Cargo.toml uv add cargo check type-check and borrow-check without producing a program (the fastest feedback) mypy, ty cargo build / cargo run ( --release ) compile / compile and run python app.py cargo test unit, integration and documentation tests (section 14) pytest cargo clippy the linter: hundreds of lints, many teaching idioms ruff check cargo fmt the formatter (there is one style) ruff format cargo doc --open HTML docs for your crate and every dependency (none built in) Clippy is the fastest way to learn idioms.

Dependencies, versions, lock file Cargo.toml lists dependencies with version requirements; Cargo.lock pins the exact versions resolved, like uv.lock .
Commit it. serde = "1.0" means "compatible with 1.0": any 1.x.
For 0.x versions the minor number is the breaking one : "0.14" accepts 0.14.9 but not 0.15.0 ( Cargo book, SemVer compatibility ).
Much of the ecosystem is at 0.x, so this matters.
Two incompatible versions of one crate can both end up in your program (say rand 0.8 and 0.9).
That avoids dependency deadlock, at the cost of a confusing error: two types with the same name that are not the same type.
Features are optional parts of a crate switched on at compile time: serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] } .
They are unified: if any crate in the build turns one on, everyone gets it.

Build scripts ( build.rs ) and procedural macros run code at build time, the same trust question as a Python package's setup code. cargo audit checks the lock file against the RustSec advisory database.

Variables, mutability, shadowing vars.rs fn main() { let x = 5; // immutable by default let mut y = 5; // `mut` makes it changeable y += 1; let spaces = " " ; // shadowing: a new variable with the same name... let spaces = spaces.len(); // ...may even have a different type const MAX_TOKENS: u32 = 4_096; // a compile-time constant, type required println!
( "x={x} y={y} spaces={spaces} max={MAX_TOKENS}" ); let z; // declared now, assigned once later if y > 5 { z = "big" } else { z = "small" } println!
( "z={z}" ); } $ rustc --edition 2024 vars.rs && ./vars x=5 y=6 spaces=3 max=4096 z=big let introduces a variable.
Its type is inferred from use, like Python, but fixed at compile time: y is an i32 (the default integer type) forever.

Change it and the compiler refuses: $ rustc --edition 2024 vars_err.rs error[E0384]: cannot assign twice to immutable variable `count` --> vars_err.rs:3:5 | 2 | let count = 0; | ----- first assignment to `count` 3 | count += 1; | ^^^^^^^^^^ cannot assign twice to immutable variable | help: consider making this binding mutable | 2 | let mut count = 0; | +++ error: aborting due to 1 previous error For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0384`. [exit code 1] This is the shape of every Rust error: a code ( E0384 ; rustc --explain E0384 prints a page about it), the file and line, the source with labels under the relevant spans, and usually a help with the fix ( +++ marks inserted text).
Shadowing : a second let spaces makes a new variable that hides the old one, even with a new type.
Useful for "parse this string into a number and keep the name"; it is not mutation.
Rust is expression-based : if , match and blocks { ... } produce values.

A block's value is its last expression without a semicolon, which is why functions end in sum rather than return sum; . println! ends in ! because it is a macro : code that writes code at compile time. {x} in the format string is like an f-string; {:?} prints the debug form (like repr ), {:#?} pretty-prints it.
Numbers: fixed widths, checked overflow Python's int grows as needed.
Rust's integers are the machine's: i8 i16 i32 i64 i128 (signed) and u8 ... u128 (unsigned), plus usize / isize , the pointer-sized types used for lengths and indexes (64 bits here).
Floats are f32 and f64 .

Nothing converts implicitly, not even u32 to f64 : $ rustc --edition 2024 mix_err.rs error[E0277]: cannot multiply `u32` by `f64` --> mix_err.rs:4:27 | 4 | println!("{}", tokens * ratio); | ^ no implementation for `u32 * f64` | = help: the trait `Mul<f64>` is not implemented for `u32` = help: the following other types implement trait `Mul<Rhs>`: `&u32` implements `Mul<u32>` `&u32` implements `Mul` `u32` implements `Mul<&u32>` `u32` implements `Mul<Duration>` `u32` implements `Mul` error: aborting due to 1 previous error For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0277`. [exit code 1] The fix is an explicit conversion: tokens as f64 * ratio , or f64::from(tokens) .

What happens at the edge of a type's range: overflow.rs fn main() { // read the value at run time so the compiler cannot see the overflow coming let x: u8 = std::env::args().nth(1).unwrap().parse().unwrap(); println!
( "checked_add: {:?}" , x.checked_add(1)); println!
( "wrapping_add: {}" , x.wrapping_add(1)); println!
( "saturating_add: {}" , x.saturating_add(1)); println!
( "overflowing_add:{:?}" , x.overflowing_add(1)); let y = x + 1; // plain +: panics in a debug build, wraps in a release build println!

( "x + 1 = {y}" ); } Predict, then reveal: In a debug build, what does ./overflow 255 print on its last line? $ rustc --edition 2024 overflow.rs && ./overflow 254 && ./overflow 255 checked_add: Some(255) wrapping_add: 255 saturating_add: 255 overflowing_add:(255, false) x + 1 = 255 checked_add: None wrapping_add: 0 saturating_add: 255 overflowing_add:(0, true) thread 'main' (16488861) panicked at overflow.rs:8:13: attempt to add with overflow note: run with `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` environment variable to display a backtrace [exit code 101] Predict, then reveal: And in a release build ( -O )? $ rustc --edition 2024 -O overflow.rs && ./overflow 255 checked_add: None wrapping_add: 0 saturating_add: 255 overflowing_add:(0, true) x + 1 = 0 This is the documented rule ( Rust Book 3.2, Integer Overflow ): debug builds check and panic; release builds wrap with two's complement and "relying on integer overflow's wrapping behavior is considered an error".
When overflow is possible, say what you want: checked_* (an Option ), wrapping_* , saturating_* or overflowing_* .
A panic is Rust's crash for bugs: it prints the message and location, unwinds the thread and exits with code 101.

If the compiler can see the overflow, it refuses outright: $ rustc --edition 2024 overflow_const.rs error: this arithmetic operation will overflow --> overflow_const.rs:2:17 | 2 | let x: u8 = 255 + 1; | ^^^^^^^ attempt to compute `u8::MAX + 1_u8`, which would overflow | = note: `#[deny(arithmetic_overflow)]` on by default error: aborting due to 1 previous error [exit code 1] The arithmetic differences that bite Python programmers, recorded: $ rustc --edition 2024 numbers.rs && ./numbers i32 range -2147483648 ..

2147483647 u64::MAX 18446744073709551615 -7 / 2 -3 -7 % 2 -1 (-7i32).div_euclid(2) -4 (-7i32).rem_euclid(2) 1 7 / 2 3 7.0 / 2.0 3.5 0.1 + 0.2 0.30000000000000004 300i32 as u8 44 -1i32 as u32 4294967295 3.99f64 as i32 3 1e20f64 as i32 2147483647 f64::NAN as i32 0 u8::try_from(300i32) Err(TryFromIntError(PosOverflow)) usize bits 64 2u64.pow(40) 1099511627776 n as f64 / 2.0 1.5 $ python3.14 numbers.py -7 // 2 -4 -7 % 2 1 int(-3.5) -3 7 / 2 3.5 0.1 + 0.2 0.30000000000000004 2**64 18446744073709551616 255 + 1 256 Integer / truncates toward zero ( -7 / 2 is -3 , Python's // gives -4 ); div_euclid and rem_euclid give Python's answers for positive divisors. as never fails: it truncates integers ( 300 as u8 is 44), reinterprets signs ( -1 as u32 is 4294967295), and saturates float to integer (not-a-number becomes 0).
Use TryFrom when a value might not fit.
Floats are the same IEEE 754 doubles as Python's: 0.1 + 0.2 prints the same.
Ownership and moves First, where values live.
Each function call gets a stack frame , a block of memory for its local variables, released automatically when the function returns.
Data whose size is only known at run time (a growing vector, a string read from a file) goes on the heap , which someone must release explicitly.
A Rust String or Vec is a small fixed-size header on the stack (three machine words: a pointer to the heap buffer, the capacity, the length; 24 bytes) plus a buffer on the heap .
Python hides all of this: every object is on the heap and names are references to it.

The ownership rules ( Rust Book 4.1 ): each value has one owner (a variable, a field, a vector slot); when the owner goes out of scope the value is dropped (its heap memory freed); assigning or passing a value moves ownership. move.rs fn shout(s: String) -> String { // takes ownership of s; returns ownership of a new String s.to_uppercase() } fn main() { let a = String:: from ( "hello" ); let b = a; // move: b now owns the heap buffer println!
( "b = {b}" ); let c = b.clone(); // explicit deep copy: a second heap buffer let d = shout(b); // b moves into the function println!
( "c = {c}, d = {d}" ); let n = 5; // i32 is Copy: assignment copies the bits let m = n; println!

( "n = {n}, m = {m}" ); // both still usable } $ rustc --edition 2024 move.rs && ./move b = hello c = hello, d = HELLO n = 5, m = 5 After let b = a; the 24-byte header was copied into b and a became unusable.
The heap buffer was not copied and not freed: it now has exactly one owner again.

Using a afterwards is refused: $ rustc --edition 2024 move_err.rs error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `a` --> move_err.rs:4:16 | 2 | let a = String::from("hello"); | - move occurs because `a` has type `String`, which does not implement the `Copy` trait 3 | let b = a; | - value moved here 4 | println!("{a} {b}"); | ^ value borrowed here after move | help: consider cloning the value if the performance cost is acceptable | 3 | let b = a.clone(); | ++++++++ error: aborting due to 1 previous error For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0382`. [exit code 1] The Python bridge In Python, b = a makes two names for one object, kept alive by a reference count.
Rust refuses the second name, so it never needs a count: the single owner frees the buffer at a point the compiler knows.
Think of a move as handing over the only key.

Copy types (integers, floats, bool , char , and tuples or arrays of them) have no heap part, so assignment copies the bits and both stay usable ( n and m above). clone() is the explicit deep copy: a second heap buffer.
It is visible in the code on purpose, so you can see every place that copies data.
Passing to a function moves too ( shout(b) ); returning moves ownership back out.
Drop: cleanup at a known moment A type can run code when it is dropped by implementing the Drop trait, which is how files close, locks release and buffers free themselves.
There is no garbage collector, so the order is fixed: drop.rs struct Noisy(& 'static str); impl Drop for Noisy { fn drop(& mut self ) { println!
( "drop {}" , self .0); } } fn consume(n: Noisy) { println!
( "consume got {}" , n.0); } // n is dropped here, at the end of the function that owns it fn main() { let _a = Noisy( "a" ); let b = Noisy( "b" ); { let _c = Noisy( "c" ); println!
( "inner scope ends" ); } // c dropped here consume(b); // b moved into consume; dropped inside it let _d = Noisy( "d" ); println!

( "main ends" ); } // locals dropped in reverse order of declaration: d, then a Predict, then reveal: In what order are the four drop lines printed? $ rustc --edition 2024 drop.rs && ./drop inner scope ends drop c consume got b drop b main ends drop d drop a Locals drop at the end of their scope in reverse order of declaration; a value moved into a function drops at the end of that function.
This is C++'s RAII (resource acquisition is initialisation) made the default; Python's equivalent is with , which you have to remember to write.

See it drawn: Ownership, animated steps through one Vec being borrowed, grown, moved, cloned and dropped, at the real stack and heap addresses recorded from a run, with the same program in Python as the "before".
Solves Use after free and double free, with no garbage collector and no reference counts.
Costs You must decide who owns each value; sharing needs borrowing (section 5) or explicit shared ownership (section 15).
Common mistake Sprinkling .clone() until it compiles.
Fine for small values; in a hot loop it allocates on every iteration.

[3, 4, 5]; let a = &v; // any number of shared borrows at once let b = &v; println!

section: 5. borrowing: many readers or one writer
text: A borrow lasts from where it is created to its last use , not to the end of the block (the Book: "a reference's scope starts from where it is introduced and continues through the last time that reference is used").

The elision rules fill in the common cases: each input reference gets its own lifetime; if there is exactly one input lifetime, outputs get it ( first_word ); in a method taking &self , outputs get self 's.

So you write lifetimes when a function has two or more reference inputs and returns a reference, or a struct stores a reference. 'static means "valid for the whole program": string literals are &'static str because they live in the program's binary.

What no lifetime can do is make a reference to a value that is about to die, because annotations describe lifetimes and never extend them: dangle_err.rs fn make_greeting(name: &str) -> &str { let s = format!

Smart pointers and interior mutability Single ownership and compile-time borrowing cover most code.

For the rest, the standard library has types that own their contents in other ways, each with a cost: Type What it gives you Cost Python analogue Box<T> one owner, value on the heap; needed for recursive types and trait objects one allocation every object Rc<T> shared ownership in one thread; freed when the last Rc goes a counter update per clone and drop reference counting Arc<T> the same across threads atomic counter updates (slower) reference counting in free-threaded CPython Cell<T> , RefCell<T> interior mutability : change through a shared reference; RefCell checks the borrow rules at run time a flag check per borrow; a panic if the rules are broken (all objects are mutable) Mutex<T> , RwLock<T> the same across threads, by locking a lock per access; contention threading.Lock Weak<T> a non-owning pointer to an Rc / Arc value; breaks cycles upgrade() may find it gone weakref A recursive type needs Box , because a value that contains itself directly would have infinite size: $ rustc --edition 2024 recursive_err.rs error[E0072]: recursive type `Expr` has infinite size --> recursive_err.rs:1:1 | 1 | enum Expr { | ^^^^^^^^^ 2 | Num(f64), 3 | Add(Expr, Expr), | ---- recursive without indirection | help: insert some indirection (e.g., a `Box`, `Rc`, or `&`) to break the cycle | 3 | Add(Box<Expr>, Expr), | ++++ + error: aborting due to 1 previous error For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0072`. [exit code 1] smart.rs use std::cell::{Cell, RefCell}; use std::rc::{Rc, Weak}; // Box: put a value on the heap.

Needed for recursive types, whose size would otherwise be infinite. #[derive(Debug)] enum Expr { Num(f64), Add(Box<Expr>, Box<Expr>), Mul(Box<Expr>, Box<Expr>), } fn eval(e: &Expr) -> f64 { match e { Expr::Num(x) => *x, Expr::Add(a, b) => eval(a) + eval(b), Expr::Mul(a, b) => eval(a) * eval(b), } } #[derive(Debug)] struct Doc { name: String, cache_hits: Cell<u32>, // interior mutability for a Copy value } fn main() { let e = Expr::Add(Box::new(Expr::Num(2.0)), Box::new(Expr::Mul(Box::new(Expr::Num(3.0)), Box::new(Expr::Num(4.0))))); println!

( "2 + 3 * 4 = {}" , eval(&e)); // Rc: shared ownership in one thread; the last owner to go frees the value let shared = Rc::new(Doc { name: "system prompt" .into(), cache_hits: Cell::new(0) }); let a = Rc::clone(&shared); // copies a pointer, bumps a counter { let b = Rc::clone(&shared); b.cache_hits.set(b.cache_hits.get() + 1); // mutate through a shared reference println!
( "strong_count inside = {}" , Rc::strong_count(&shared)); } println!

( "strong_count after = {}, hits = {}, name = {}" , Rc::strong_count(&a), a.cache_hits.get(), a.name); // RefCell: borrow rules checked at run time instead of compile time let log = Rc::new(RefCell::new(Vec::<String>::new())); let writer = Rc::clone(&log); writer.borrow_mut().push( "first" .into()); writer.borrow_mut().push( "second" .into()); println!

( "log = {:?}" , log.borrow()); // Weak: a non-owning pointer (it does not keep the value alive); used to break cycles let parent = Rc::new(String:: from ( "parent" )); let w: Weak<String> = Rc::downgrade(&parent); println!
( "weak upgrade while alive: {}" , w.upgrade().is_some()); drop(parent); println!
( "weak upgrade after drop: {}" , w.upgrade().is_some()); println!

( "size_of Box<Expr> = {}, Rc<Doc> = {}, Expr = {}" , std::mem::size_of::<Box<Expr>>(), std::mem::size_of::<Rc<Doc>>(), std::mem::size_of::<Expr>()); // The run-time check, failing: two mutable borrows at once let first = log.borrow_mut(); let second = log.borrow_mut(); // panics: already mutably borrowed println!

( "{} {}" , first.len(), second.len()); } $ rustc --edition 2024 smart.rs && ./smart 2 + 3 * 4 = 14 strong_count inside = 3 strong_count after = 2, hits = 1, name = system prompt log = ["first", "second"] weak upgrade while alive: true weak upgrade after drop: false size_of Box<Expr> = 8, Rc<Doc> = 8, Expr = 24 thread 'main' (16492202) panicked at smart.rs:58:22: RefCell already borrowed note: run with `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` environment variable to display a backtrace [exit code 101] The last line is the price of RefCell : the same rule as section 5, but discovered while the program runs.
Rc<RefCell<T>> compiles in situations where plain references would not, and it is the most common way learners make a borrow error go away and turn it into a crash.
The old page's gate for this stage: explain why Rc<RefCell<T>> compiles but can still panic.
Answer: the exclusivity check moved from compile time to run time.
Reference cycles leak Reference counting cannot free a cycle, in Rust as in Python (where the cycle collector cleans up afterwards; Rust has none).

Leaking memory is safe in Rust's sense, so the compiler allows it: leak.rs (lines 20 to 37) fn main() { { let x = node( "x (cycle of Rc)" ); let y = node( "y (cycle of Rc)" ); *x.next.borrow_mut() = Some(Rc::clone(&y)); // x -> y *y.next.borrow_mut() = Some(Rc::clone(&x)); // y -> x: a cycle println!

( "cycle: x strong_count = {}" , Rc::strong_count(&x)); } // our two handles go, but each node still owns the other: neither count reaches 0 { let x = node( "x (Weak back edge)" ); let y = node( "y (Weak back edge)" ); *x.next.borrow_mut() = Some(Rc::clone(&y)); // x owns y *y.back.borrow_mut() = Rc::downgrade(&x); // y only points back at x println!
( "weak: x strong_count = {}, weak_count = {}" , Rc::strong_count(&x), Rc::weak_count(&x)); println!
( "y.back.upgrade() is {}" , y.back.borrow().upgrade().map(|n| n.name).unwrap_or( "gone" )); } println!

( "end of main: the Rc cycle was never dropped (a leak, which safe Rust allows)" ); } Predict, then reveal: Which of the four nodes print "drop"? $ rustc --edition 2024 leak.rs && ./leak cycle: x strong_count = 2 weak: x strong_count = 1, weak_count = 1 y.back.upgrade() is x (Weak back edge) drop x (Weak back edge) drop y (Weak back edge) end of main: the Rc cycle was never dropped (a leak, which safe Rust allows) Rule of thumb: ownership should form a tree.
Back pointers (child to parent, node to previous) are Weak , or better, indexes into a Vec that owns all the nodes (an "arena"), which is how most Rust graph code is written.
Threads without data races A data race is two threads touching the same memory at the same time, at least one of them writing, with nothing ordering them.
Updates get lost or values tear.
In CPython the GIL used to hide most of these; free-threaded Python 3.14 does not, and an unsynchronised counter there loses updates (measured on the Python page ).

Rust makes data races a compile error in safe code, by applying section 5's rule across threads: shared data may be read by many threads, and changed only through a type that synchronises (a lock or an atomic).

The obvious Python translation, eight threads incrementing one counter, does not compile, and the three errors are the three problems: race_err.rs use std::thread; fn main() { let mut counter = 0u64; let mut hs = vec! []; for _ in 0..8 { hs.push(thread::spawn(|| for _ in 0..100_000 { counter += 1; })); } for h in hs { h.join().unwrap(); } println!

( "{counter}" ); } $ rustc --edition 2024 race_err.rs error[E0373]: closure may outlive the current function, but it borrows `counter`, which is owned by the current function --> race_err.rs:7:31 | 7 | hs.push(thread::spawn(|| for _ in 0..100_000 { counter += 1; })); | ^^ ------- `counter` is borrowed here | | | may outlive borrowed value `counter` | note: function requires argument type to outlive `'static` --> race_err.rs:7:17 | 7 | hs.push(thread::spawn(|| for _ in 0..100_000 { counter += 1; })); | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ help: to force the closure to take ownership of `counter` (and any other referenced variables), use the `move` keyword | 7 | hs.push(thread::spawn(move || for _ in 0..100_000 { counter += 1; })); | ++++ show the remaining 34 lines error[E0499]: cannot borrow `counter` as mutable more than once at a time --> race_err.rs:7:31 | 7 | hs.push(thread::spawn(|| for _ in 0..100_000 { counter += 1; })); | --------------^^--------------------------------------- | | | | | | | borrows occur due to use of `counter` in closure | | `counter` was mutably borrowed here in the previous iteration of the loop | argument requires that `counter` is borrowed for `'static` | note: requirement that the value outlives `'static` introduced here --> /rustc/b940084d7eb6a299eb4bfeb8e34901bc051e7ac4/library/std/src/thread/functions.rs:128:14 error[E0502]: cannot borrow `counter` as immutable because it is also borrowed as mutable --> race_err.rs:10:16 | 7 | hs.push(thread::spawn(|| for _ in 0..100_000 { counter += 1; })); | ------------------------------------------------------- | | | | | | | first borrow occurs due to use of `counter` in closure | | mutable borrow occurs here | argument requires that `counter` is borrowed for `'static` ...

10 | println!("{counter}"); | ^^^^^^^ immutable borrow occurs here | note: requirement that the value outlives `'static` introduced here --> /rustc/b940084d7eb6a299eb4bfeb8e34901bc051e7ac4/library/std/src/thread/functions.rs:128:14 error: aborting due to 3 previous errors Some errors have detailed explanations: E0373, E0499, E0502.
For more information about an error, try `rustc --explain E0373`. [exit code 1] E0373: the thread may outlive counter (a spawned thread is not joined automatically).
E0499: eight closures would each hold &mut counter at once.

Scoped threads fix the first problem but not the second, which is the data race itself: $ rustc --edition 2024 race_scope_err.rs error[E0499]: cannot borrow `counter` as mutable more than once at a time --> race_scope_err.rs:7:21 | 5 | thread::scope(|s| { | - has type `&'1 Scope<'1, '_>` 6 | for _ in 0..8 { 7 | s.spawn(|| for _ in 0..100_000 { counter += 1; }); | --------^^--------------------------------------- | | | | | | | borrows occur due to use of `counter` in closure | | `counter` was mutably borrowed here in the previous iteration of the loop | argument requires that `counter` is borrowed for `'1` | note: requirement that the value outlives `'1` introduced here --> /rustc/b940084d7eb6a299eb4bfeb8e34901bc051e7ac4/library/std/src/thread/scoped.rs:203:34 error: aborting due to 1 previous error For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0499`. [exit code 1] Two marker traits carry the rule.
They are implemented automatically by the compiler for types whose parts qualify ( std::marker::Send ): Send : a value of this type may be moved to another thread.
Sync : a &T may be shared between threads (precisely, T is Sync if &T is Send ).
Rc is neither, because two threads updating its non-atomic counter at once would be a race; Arc uses atomic updates and is both.

Try to send an Rc : $ rustc --edition 2024 rc_thread_err.rs error[E0277]: `Rc<Vec<i32>>` cannot be sent between threads safely --> rc_thread_err.rs:7:27 | 7 | let h = thread::spawn(move || s2.len()); | ------------- -------^^^^^^^^^ | | | | | `Rc<Vec<i32>>` cannot be sent between threads safely | | within this `{closure@rc_thread_err.rs:7:27: 7:34}` | required by a bound introduced by this call | = help: within `{closure@rc_thread_err.rs:7:27: 7:34}`, the trait `Send` is not implemented for `Rc<Vec<i32>>` note: required because it's used within this closure --> rc_thread_err.rs:7:27 | 7 | let h = thread::spawn(move || s2.len()); | ^^^^^^^ note: required by a bound in `spawn` --> /rustc/b940084d7eb6a299eb4bfeb8e34901bc051e7ac4/library/std/src/thread/functions.rs:125:0 show the remaining 5 lines error: aborting due to 1 previous error For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0277`. [exit code 1] The working toolbox, every result exact: threads.rs use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicU64, Ordering}; use std::sync::mpsc; use std::sync::{Arc, Mutex}; use std::thread; fn main() { // 1. spawn + join; `move` gives the thread its own copy of what it uses let docs = vec! [ "a b c" , "d e" , "f" ]; let handles: Vec<_> = docs.into_iter().enumerate().map(|(i, d)| { thread::spawn( move || (i, d.split_whitespace().count())) }).collect(); let counts: Vec<_> = handles.into_iter().map(|h| h.join().unwrap()).collect(); println!

( "spawned: {counts:?}" ); // 2. scoped threads may borrow local data, because they are joined before the scope ends let data = vec! [1u64; 1_000_000]; let (left, right) = data.split_at(data.len() / 2); let total = thread::scope(|s| { let a = s.spawn(|| left.iter().sum::<u64>()); let b = s.spawn(|| right.iter().sum::<u64>()); a.join().unwrap() + b.join().unwrap() }); println!

( "scoped sum: {total}" ); // 3. shared mutable state: Arc (shared ownership across threads) + Mutex (one writer at a time) let counter = Arc::new(Mutex::new(0u64)); let mut hs = vec! []; for _ in 0..8 { let c = Arc::clone(&counter); hs.push(thread::spawn( move || for _ in 0..100_000 { *c.lock().unwrap() += 1; })); } for h in hs { h.join().unwrap(); } println!

( "mutex counter: {} (expected 800000)" , *counter.lock().unwrap()); // 4. an atomic does the same without a lock let hits = Arc::new(AtomicU64::new(0)); thread::scope(|s| for _ in 0..8 { let h = &hits; s.spawn( move || for _ in 0..100_000 { h.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed); }); }); println!

( "atomic counter: {}" , hits.load(Ordering::Relaxed)); // 5. channels: send values from many producers to one consumer let (tx, rx) = mpsc::channel(); for id in 0..3 { let tx = tx.clone(); thread::spawn( move || tx.send( format!
( "worker {id} done" )).unwrap()); } drop(tx); // close our copy so the loop below ends when the workers finish let mut got: Vec<String> = rx.iter().collect(); got.sort(); println!

( "channel: {got:?}" ); } $ rustc --edition 2024 threads.rs && ./threads spawned: [(0, 3), (1, 2), (2, 1)] scoped sum: 1000000 mutex counter: 800000 (expected 800000) atomic counter: 800000 channel: ["worker 0 done", "worker 1 done", "worker 2 done"] thread::spawn(move || ...) plus join() for owned work; thread::scope when threads should borrow local data.
Arc<Mutex<T>> for shared mutable state: lock() returns a guard that unlocks when dropped, and the data is reachable only through the guard, so you cannot forget the lock.
Atomics ( AtomicU64 ) for single counters and flags.
Channels ( mpsc ) to pass messages instead of sharing memory.
For data parallelism over a collection, the rayon crate turns iter() into par_iter() ; Part 2 uses it to parallelise the token counter inside a Python extension ( Part 2 ).

What the compiler does not prevent Deadlocks (two threads each holding the lock the other needs), logic races (check-then-act with the lock released in between), and leaked memory are all possible in safe Rust. "Fearless" means no data races and no use after free, not no concurrency bugs.
Async, in one paragraph Threads suit CPU work.

For thousands of concurrent network calls (an LLM gateway, an agent fanning out tool calls), Rust uses async fn and .await , as Python's asyncio does, with two differences worth knowing now: a future does nothing until it is awaited or spawned (calling an async fn does not start it), and the language ships no event loop, so you choose a runtime library, almost always tokio .
Part 3, Services and CLIs teaches async from zero and builds an HTTP service with it.
17. unsafe, in one section Some correct code cannot be proved safe by the compiler: the inside of Vec , calls into C libraries, hardware access.

Inside an unsafe block you may do five extra things, the "unsafe superpowers" ( Rust Book 20.1 ): dereference a raw pointer; call an unsafe function; access or modify a mutable static ; implement an unsafe trait; access fields of a union .

Nothing else changes: " unsafe doesn't turn off the borrow checker or disable any of Rust's other safety checks". unsafe_ok.rs fn main() { let v = vec! [10u32, 20, 30]; let p: * const u32 = v.as_ptr(); // making a raw pointer is safe let second = unsafe { *p.add(1) }; // dereferencing it is not: we promise it is in bounds println!

( "second = {second}" ); // A safe API built on unsafe: split_at_mut hands out two &mut halves of one slice, // which the borrow checker cannot prove disjoint by itself. let mut a = [1, 2, 3, 4]; let (l, r) = a.split_at_mut(2); l[0] += 100; r[0] += 100; println!

( "{a:?}" ); } $ rustc --edition 2024 unsafe_ok.rs && ./unsafe_ok second = 20 [101, 2, 103, 4] Without the block, the compiler refuses and says why each operation needs it: $ rustc --edition 2024 unsafe_deref_err.rs error[E0133]: dereference of raw pointer is unsafe and requires unsafe block --> unsafe_deref_err.rs:4:20 | 4 | println!("{}", *p.add(1)); | ^^^^^^^^^ dereference of raw pointer | = note: raw pointers may be null, dangling or unaligned; they can violate aliasing rules and cause data races: all of these are undefined behavior error[E0133]: call to unsafe function `std::ptr::const_ptr::<impl *const T>::add` is unsafe and requires unsafe block --> unsafe_deref_err.rs:4:21 | 4 | println!("{}", *p.add(1)); | ^^^^^^^^ call to unsafe function | = note: consult the function's documentation for information on how to avoid undefined behavior error: aborting due to 2 previous errors For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0133`. [exit code 1] The pattern to aim for is the one split_at_mut shows: a small unsafe core with a stated invariant ("the two halves never overlap"), wrapped in a safe API that cannot be used to break it.
Because unsafe is a keyword, every such place can be found with a text search and reviewed.
When you get it wrong: Miri Breaking an invariant is undefined behaviour , exactly as in C++: the program may do anything, including appear to work.

This program reads one element past the end of a vector, and then reads a freed vector; built in release mode, it runs and prints plausible numbers: main.rs // Undefined behaviour that compiles and "works": reading one element past the end // through a raw pointer, and using a pointer after its Vec was freed. fn main() { let v = vec! [10u32, 20, 30]; let p = v.as_ptr(); let past_end = unsafe { *p.add(3) }; // out of bounds: UB println!
( "read past the end: {past_end}" ); let q = { let w = vec! [1u32, 2, 3]; w.as_ptr() }; // w freed here; q dangles let after_free = unsafe { *q }; // use after free: UB println!

( "read after free: {after_free}" ); } $ cargo run -q --release read past the end: 0 read after free: 0 Miri is an interpreter for Rust's intermediate representation that checks every memory access against the rules.

It runs on the nightly toolchain (here rustc 1.101.0-nightly of 2026-10-04) and is much slower than native code, so you run your tests under it, not production: $ cargo +nightly miri run -q 2>&1 | grep -v "^Preparing a sysroot" error: Undefined Behavior: memory access failed: attempting to access 4 bytes, but got alloc291+0xc which is at or beyond the end of the allocation of size 12 bytes --> src/main.rs:6:29 | 6 | let past_end = unsafe { *p.add(3) }; // out of bounds: UB | ^^^^^^^^^ Undefined Behavior occurred here | = help: this indicates a bug in the program: it performed an invalid operation, and caused Undefined Behavior = help: see https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/behavior-considered-undefined.html for further information help: alloc291 was allocated here: --> src/main.rs:4:13 | 4 | let v = vec![10u32, 20, 30]; | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ note: some details are omitted, run with `MIRIFLAGS=-Zmiri-backtrace=full` for a verbose backtrace error: aborting due to 1 previous error It stops at the first violation, names it ( at or beyond the end of the allocation of size 12 bytes ) and points at where the memory was allocated.
If you write unsafe , run cargo +nightly miri test in CI.
The C++ page's equivalent tools are the sanitizers ( C++ page, Part 1 ).
Use it for FFI (calling C), performance-critical data structures, and building safe abstractions the checker cannot verify.
Costs You take on C's obligations for that block; reviewers must check the invariant by hand.
Do not Use unsafe to silence a borrow error.
If safe code cannot express it, the design usually needs an index, a RefCell or a different owner.
If you know some C++ Optional.
Rust's ownership is C++'s RAII plus move semantics, with the compiler enforcing what the C++ Core Guidelines only recommend ( C++ page , Part 1, teaches the C++ side).

C++ Rust The difference auto b = std::move(a); let b = a; Moves are the default and the moved-from variable is unusable (a compile error), not "valid but unspecified". destructor impl Drop Same deterministic order (reverse of declaration). const T& , T& &T , &mut T Aliasing XOR mutation is checked, so iterator invalidation and dangling references do not compile. std::string_view into a temporary &str with a lifetime Undefined behaviour in C++; E0515 or E0597 in Rust. templates, concepts generics with trait bounds Both monomorphise; Rust checks the generic body against the bounds once, at definition, so errors are short. virtual dyn Trait Opt-in at the use site, no inheritance; the vtable pointer lives in the fat pointer, not in the object. unique_ptr , shared_ptr Box , Rc / Arc Rc is a non-atomic shared_ptr , allowed only on one thread (not Send ). exceptions, std::expected Result and ?
Panics exist but are for bugs. everything unsafe { } C++'s rules apply only inside the block, and the block is searchable.
No function overloading and no implicit conversions; prefer indexes and arenas to pointer graphs, because self-referential structs are the design Rust refuses.

Functions and modules: #[pyfunction] , #[pymodule] Step 1 of the token counter: the Rosetta token loop as plain Rust, and a thin function Python can call. ext/src/lib.rs /// Tokens = maximal runs of ASCII letters or digits (rule 3 of PROGRAM.md). /// Non-ASCII characters are UTF-8 bytes >= 0x80, so a byte loop gives the char answer. fn tokens(s: &[u8]) -> u64 { let mut n = 0; let mut inside = false ; for &b in s { let t = b.is_ascii_alphanumeric(); if t && !inside { n += 1; } inside = t; } n } ext/src/lib.rs /// Step 1: one message per call. `&str` borrows the Python string's UTF-8 bytes. #[pyfunction] fn count_tokens(text: &str) -> u64 { tokens(text.as_bytes()) } #[pyfunction] generates the glue: a C-level function that takes Python's argument objects, converts each one to the Rust parameter type ( &str here), calls your function, and converts the return value ( u64 ) back into a Python int .
The /// doc comment becomes the Python docstring.

(1) PyO3 adds a note naming the parameter ( while processing 'text' , shown by Python 3.11+ as an exception note).
(2) &Bound<PyList> accepts exactly a list , so a tuple is refused, while Vec<String> accepts any sequence (a tuple worked) but deliberately refuses a str , which is also a sequence and a classic bug.
(3) Inside count_many the item check runs after argument parsing, so its error has no note: say which item failed in your own messages.
(4) A str holding a lone surrogate (legal in Python, not in UTF-8) cannot become &str and raises UnicodeEncodeError .
The types in those signatures Rust type What it is Python analogy Python<'py> A zero-size token proving this thread is attached to the interpreter (holds the GIL on a normal build).
You get it as a parameter or from a Bound .
Being inside the interpreter at all; Python code always is Bound<'py, T> A strong reference to a Python object of type T ( PyList , PyDict , PyAny ), usable only while attached.
Dropping it decrements the refcount.
Any ordinary variable holding an object Py<T> The same reference without the 'py lifetime: can be stored in a struct or sent to another thread; call .bind(py) to use it.

An object kept in a global or a queue PyResult<T> Result<T, PyErr> : Err becomes a raised exception (section 6). return or raise The 'py is a lifetime ( Part 1 , section 6, explains them): the compiler uses it to stop a Bound escaping the region where the interpreter is attached.
You rarely write it out except in return types like Bound<'py, PyDict> .

text: Crossing the boundary: what each conversion costs A Python str and a Rust String are different things in memory.

section: 4. crossing the boundary: what each conversion costs
text: A Python str is an object on Python's heap with a refcount, a length and its characters in one of three fixed widths (1, 2 or 4 bytes each, whichever fits the widest character).

section: 4. crossing the boundary: what each conversion costs
text: A Rust &str is just a pointer and a length into UTF-8 bytes ( Part 1 , section 7: String against &str ).

section: 4. crossing the boundary: what each conversion costs
text: So every argument crosses the boundary in one of two ways: Borrowed (a view): Rust gets a pointer into memory Python owns. &str from a str , &[u8] from bytes , a NumPy array view.

section: 4. crossing the boundary: what each conversion costs
text: No allocation, no copy, but the view only lives for the call.

section: 4. crossing the boundary: what each conversion costs
text: Owned (a copy): Rust builds its own value.

section: 4. crossing the boundary: what each conversion costs
text: String , Vec<T> , HashMap<K, V> : one allocation per string, one conversion per element.

text: The Crossing the boundary tab animates one call with three messages, step by step, copied against borrowed, with counters for bytes copied and objects created.
NumPy arrays without copies (rust-numpy) A Python list of floats is an array of pointers to separate float objects, each 24 bytes with its own refcount; converting it means visiting every object.
A NumPy array is one contiguous block of raw f64 values plus a small header (shape, strides, dtype).

The numpy crate (rust-numpy, 0.29.0, the release matching PyO3 0.29) lets Rust read that block in place: ext/src/lib.rs /// Sum of squares from a Python list: every float is converted into a new Vec<f64>. #[pyfunction] fn sum_sq_list(xs: Vec<f64>) -> f64 { xs.iter().map(|x| x * x).sum() } /// The same from a NumPy array: a read-only view of NumPy's own buffer, zero copies. #[pyfunction] fn sum_sq_array(xs: PyReadonlyArray1<'_, f64>) -> PyResult<f64> { let s = xs.as_slice()?; // error if the array is not contiguous Ok(s.iter().map(|x| x * x).sum()) } /// Returning results: a Vec<u64> becomes a Python list (one int object per element) ... #[pyfunction] fn counts_list(texts: &Bound<'_, PyList>) -> PyResult<Vec<u64>> { count_many(texts) } /// ... or a NumPy array that takes over the Vec's buffer without copying it. #[pyfunction] fn counts_array<'py>(py: Python<'py>, texts: &Bound<'py, PyList>) -> PyResult<Bound<'py, PyArray1<u64>>> { Ok(count_many(texts)?.into_pyarray(py)) } /// Dicts: `HashMap<String, u64>` copies every key into a new String ... #[pyfunction] fn dict_total_owned(d: HashMap<String, u64>) -> u64 { d.values().sum() } /// ... while iterating the `PyDict` in place only reads the values. #[pyfunction] fn dict_total(d: &Bound<'_, PyDict>) -> PyResult<u64> { let mut s = 0; for (_k, v) in d.iter() { s += v.extract::<u64>()?; } Ok(s) } PyReadonlyArray1<f64> checks the dtype and takes a shared borrow of the array (rust-numpy tracks borrows so Rust cannot write to an array Python code also holds as read-only); as_slice() gives a plain &[f64] when the memory is contiguous.
On a million floats: list ns per element, array ns.
Rust lost to NumPy here, and that is the lesson np.dot(x, x) took ns per element, x faster than the Rust loop.

The Rust compiler may not reorder floating-point additions (the result would change in the last bits), so .sum() runs one add at a time; NumPy calls a BLAS routine that keeps several partial sums in SIMD registers.
Do not port what NumPy, PyTorch or polars already do; port the loops they cannot express.

section: 7. classes: #[pyclass] keeps rust state between calls
text: A #[pyclass] is how: a Rust struct that Python sees as a class.

section: 7. classes: #[pyclass] keeps rust state between calls
text: The Python object owns the struct; methods run on it in place, so the per-user table never crosses the boundary until you ask for a result. ext/src/lib.rs /// A running per-user counter that lives across calls. #[pyclass(module = "tokrs" )] struct Counter { per_user: HashMap<String, u64>, lines: u64, } #[pymethods] impl Counter { #[new] fn new() -> Self { Counter { per_user: HashMap::new(), lines: 0 } } /// Add one message. `&mut self`: PyO3 checks at run time that nobody else holds it. fn add(& mut self , user: &str, text: &str) { self .lines += 1; * self .per_user.entry(user.to_owned()).or_insert(0) += tokens(text.as_bytes()); } /// The n heaviest users, ties by id (rule 5). #[pyo3(signature = (n=5))] fn top(& self , n: usize) -> Vec<(String, u64)> { let mut v: Vec<(String, u64)> = self .per_user.iter().map(|(u, c)| (u.clone(), *c)).collect(); v.sort_by(|a, b| b.1.cmp(&a.1).then_with(|| a.0.cmp(&b.0))); v.truncate(n); v } #[getter] fn total(& self ) -> u64 { self .per_user.values().sum() } fn __len__(& self ) -> usize { self .per_user.len() } fn __repr__(& self ) -> String { format!( "Counter(users={}, lines={}, tokens={})" , self .per_user.len(), self .lines, self .total()) } } #[new] is __init__ (strictly __new__ ), #[getter] makes a read-only property, and methods named like Python's special methods ( __len__ , __repr__ ) become them. &self methods read; &mut self methods write.

section: 8. releasing the gil, and parallel rust with rayon
text: Parallelism inside one call: rayon If the caller is single-threaded, Rust can split the work itself. rayon turns an iterator into a parallel one ( .into_par_iter() ) and runs it on a pool of OS threads, one per core by default; reduce merges the partial tallies: ext/src/lib.rs /// Pure Rust, no Python objects: safe to run without the GIL and on many threads. fn tally(data: &[u8], first_lineno: u64) -> Tally { let mut t = Tally::default(); for (i, line) in data.split_inclusive(|&b| b == b'\n').enumerate() { t.lines += 1; match serde_json::from_slice::<Message>(line) { Ok(m) => { t.ok += 1; *t.per_user.entry(m.user).or_insert(0) += tokens(m.text.as_bytes()); } Err(_) => { t.bad += 1; if t.first_bad == 0 { t.first_bad = first_lineno + i as u64; } } } } t } fn merge( mut a: Tally, b: Tally) -> Tally { a.lines += b.lines; a.ok += b.ok; a.bad += b.bad; if a.first_bad == 0 { a.first_bad = b.first_bad; } for (u, n) in b.per_user { *a.per_user.entry(u).or_insert(0) += n; } a } ext/src/lib.rs /// Step 5: detached and parallel. rayon splits the chunks over its thread pool. #[pyfunction] #[pyo3(signature = (data, threads=8))] fn tally_bytes_parallel<'py>(py: Python<'py>, data: &[u8], threads: usize) -> PyResult<Report<'py>> { let t = py.detach(|| { chunks(data, threads) .into_par_iter() .map(|(part, first)| tally(part, first)) .reduce(Tally::default, merge) }); to_python(py, t) } tally takes only &[u8] and returns plain Rust data, so it is safe to run on any thread; the compiler checks that too (rayon requires Send ).

text: Mistakes Detaching around a tiny function (all overhead, no gain); initialising a std::sync::OnceLock or LazyLock with code that calls Python, which can deadlock against the GIL (PyO3's FAQ: use PyOnceLock ); starting a rayon pool in a process that already runs one worker per core (oversubscription).
Free-threaded Python (3.14t) CPython 3.14 officially supports a second build without the GIL, python3.14t (PEP 779); the root's Reading and the Python page cover what it costs and what it breaks.
For extension authors it changes two things.
A module must declare that it is safe without the GIL, or importing it turns the GIL back on for the whole process.
Since PyO3 0.28 (2026-02-01) every PyO3 module declares itself safe by default; you opt out with #[pymodule(gil_used = true)] (from 0.23 to 0.27 it was the other way round).

A one-function module that opts out ( code/gilused/ ), imported after tokrs on 3.14t: $ python3.14t c10_ft.py GIL enabled at start: False after import tokrs: False after import gilused: True RuntimeWarning: The global interpreter lock (GIL) has been enabled to load module 'gilused.gilused', which has not declared that it can run safely without the GIL.
To override this behavior and keep the GIL disabled (at your own risk), run with PYTHON_GIL=0 or -Xgil=0.
Calls really do run at the same time, so state shared between threads must be protected by Rust, not by the GIL. tokrs functions that only read their arguments are fine.
The Counter class of section 7 is not: its add takes &mut self , and PyO3's run-time borrow flag now sees two threads asking for it at once.

Eight threads, one shared Counter , 20,000 add calls each: $ python3.14t c13_ft_borrow.py, then python3.14 c13_ft_borrow.py GIL enabled: False Counter: 160000 calls, added 139164, raised 20836 Already borrowed SharedCounter: 160000 calls, added 160000, raised 0 GIL enabled: True Counter: 160000 calls, added 160000, raised 0 SharedCounter: 160000 calls, added 160000, raised 0 Nothing was corrupted (Rust's guarantee held: added plus raised equals 160,000), but on 3.14t 13% of the calls failed (22% to 27% in three earlier runs of the same script) with RuntimeError: Already borrowed , and the same script on the GIL build never fails, which is how this bug hides in testing.

The fix is the Rust way of sharing: make the class frozen (no &mut self , so no borrow flag) and put the mutable part behind a Mutex , which makes threads wait their turn instead of failing ( Part 1 , sections 15 and 16, covers Mutex and Send ): ext/src/lib.rs /// The thread-safe version: `frozen` means no `&mut self` ever, so PyO3 needs no /// run-time borrow flag; the mutable state sits behind a Mutex that threads queue on. #[pyclass(module = "tokrs" , frozen)] struct SharedCounter { per_user: std::sync::Mutex<HashMap<String, u64>>, } #[pymethods] impl SharedCounter { #[new] fn new() -> Self { SharedCounter { per_user: std::sync::Mutex::new(HashMap::new()) } } fn add(& self , user: &str, text: &str) { let n = tokens(text.as_bytes()); // count outside the lock * self .per_user.lock().unwrap().entry(user.to_owned()).or_insert(0) += n; } #[getter] fn total(& self ) -> u64 { self .per_user.lock().unwrap().values().sum() } } The token counting happens before lock() , so threads only queue for the short dictionary update.
PyO3's guide has the full checklist ( free-threading , pyclass thread safety ), and py-free-threading.github.io tracks which libraries are ready.
PyO3 0.29 supports 3.14t and later only (it dropped 3.13t, which CPython never declared supported).

Type stubs and tests A compiled module has no Python source, so mypy, ty and your editor cannot see its signatures.
You give them a stub file ( .pyi ): Python syntax with ... for bodies, read only by type checkers.

For a project like this one (Rust only, no Python package directory), maturin picks up <module>.pyi next to Cargo.toml and adds it to the wheel with a py.typed marker ( maturin: adding Python type information ).

Common mistakes Timing a debug build maturin develop without --release builds without optimisation.
Always benchmark release builds.
One call per element Each crossing costs about as much as counting a 125-character message (section 4).
Pass the list, return a list or an array.
Porting one function inside a Python hot path The rest of the path still runs in Python (section 1).
Move the whole path, or measure what is left first.
Owned types everywhere Vec<String> , HashMap and Vec<f64> copy; use &str , &[u8] , &Bound<PyList> , NumPy views unless Rust must keep the data.
Holding the GIL through long Rust work Other Python threads stop (section 8).
Wrap pure-Rust work in py.detach .
A &mut self class shared between threads Works on the GIL build, raises Already borrowed on 3.14t (section 9).
Use frozen plus a Mutex or atomics, and run tests on 3.14t.
Catching PanicException with except Exception It derives from BaseException .
A panic is a bug: return PyResult instead.
Forgetting to restart Python after a rebuild A process cannot unload a shared library it has loaded, so importlib.reload will not pick up the new build.
Restart the interpreter or notebook kernel.
Module name mismatch The #[pymodule] name, the library name in Cargo.toml and module-name in pyproject.toml must agree, or import fails because CPython cannot find PyInit_<name> .
Rewriting NumPy A plain Rust loop lost to np.dot by x (section 5).
Shipping only an abi3 wheel Free-threaded users cannot install it (section 12): add cp314t wheels, or abi3t once you can require 3.15.
No stub file Type checkers then know nothing about your module (section 11).

The three ideas to keep from this part.
(1) A Rust tool or service is one compiled file : that is most of why people write them.

A CLI with clap The problem it solves.
A command-line tool has to read arguments, validate them, print help, report errors on stderr, write results on stdout, and return an exit code a shell script can test.
Doing that by hand is tedious and always slightly wrong. clap generates all of it from a struct.

Arguments are a struct tok/src/bin/tokcount.rs (lines 10 to 37) /// Count word-ish tokens per user in JSONL chat logs. #[derive(Parser)] #[command(name = "tokcount", version)] struct Cli { #[command(subcommand)] cmd: Cmd, } #[derive(Subcommand)] enum Cmd { /// Count tokens per user in one or more JSONL files ("-" reads stdin) Count { /// Input files; "-" means standard input #[arg(required = true)] files: Vec<PathBuf>, /// How many users to list #[arg(short = 'n', long, default_value_t = 5, value_parser = clap::value_parser!(u16).range(1..=1000))] top: u16, /// Print JSON instead of text #[arg(long)] json: bool, /// Exit with code 3 if any line is malformed #[arg(long)] strict: bool, }, /// Count tokens in a piece of text (an argument, or stdin when absent) Text { text: Option<String> }, } Read it like a typed argparse declaration. #[derive(Parser)] is a derive macro : at compile time it writes the parsing code for this struct.

That is fine: libSystem is on every Mac.
Linux: the usual target links glibc dynamically, so a binary built on a new distribution can fail on an old one.
The *-unknown-linux-musl targets link the musl C library statically: one file that runs on any Linux kernel of that architecture, and the input for the empty container image below.

Async Rust from zero The problem it solves.
A service spends most of its time waiting: for the network, a database, a model API.
One OS thread per waiting request works up to a few thousand requests, then the memory for stacks and the cost of switching threads dominate.
Async lets one thread juggle many waiting operations: each operation runs until it would wait, hands the thread back, and is resumed when its data arrives.
Python's asyncio and JavaScript's event loop are the same idea; the Python page's Part 1 teaches asyncio from the event loop up ( Python page , tab "Event loop").
Rust's version differs in three ways, each shown below with real runs: futures are lazy , the runtime is a library you choose (and usually runs on several threads ), and cancellation is dropping .
A future is a value, and it is lazy An async fn does not run when you call it.

It returns a future : a value that describes the work, which runs only when something polls it, normally .await . tok/examples/a1_lazy.rs // A future is a value: calling an async fn runs nothing until something awaits (polls) it. async fn hello(tag: &str) -> u32 { println!
( " {tag}: body runs" ); 42 } #[tokio::main(flavor = "current_thread")] async fn main() { println!

( "2. holding a future of {} bytes; its body has not run" , std::mem::size_of_val(&fut)); let v = fut. await ; // now the runtime polls it to completion println!
( "3. awaited it: {v}" ); hello( "b" ); // never awaited: the compiler warns and the body never runs println!
( "4. end of main" ); } Predict, then reveal: What prints between line 1 and line 3?

What .await does: poll, Pending, wake Every future implements one method, poll .

The runtime calls it; it returns Poll::Ready(value) if done, or Poll::Pending if it has to wait, after arranging for a waker to be called when it can make progress (a socket becomes readable, a timer fires).
The runtime then polls something else, and polls this future again only after its waker fires.
That is the whole protocol.

A hand-written future, to see it: tok/examples/a1_poll.rs // What .await does underneath: the runtime calls poll() until it returns Ready. // A hand-written future that is not ready the first two times it is polled. use std::future::Future; use std::pin::Pin; use std::task::{Context, Poll}; struct Countdown { left: u32, } impl Future for Countdown { type Output = & 'static str; fn poll( mut self : Pin<& mut Self >, cx: & mut Context< '_ >) -> Poll< Self ::Output> { if self .left == 0 { println!
( " poll: Ready" ); return Poll::Ready( "done" ); } println!

( " poll: Pending ({} left), asking to be woken" , self .left); self .left -= 1; // A real future (a socket, a timer) hands the waker to the OS event source. // Here we wake ourselves at once, so the runtime polls again. cx.waker().wake_by_ref(); Poll::Pending } } #[tokio::main(flavor = "current_thread")] async fn main() { println!
( "awaiting Countdown {{ left: 2 }}" ); let r = Countdown { left: 2 }. await ; println!

( "result: {r}" ); } awaiting Countdown { left: 2 } poll: Pending (2 left), asking to be woken poll: Pending (1 left), asking to be woken poll: Ready result: done You will almost never write poll yourself; async fn generates it, with one state per .await point.

Two consequences matter every day: code between two awaits runs without interruption (no other task can run on that thread meanwhile), and a future that is never polled again simply stops at its last await.
Pin, in one paragraph.
The generated state machine can hold a reference to one of its own local variables across an await (a buffer and a slice of it).

If the future were moved in memory, that reference would dangle. poll therefore takes Pin<&mut Self> : a pointer that promises the future will not move again once polled. .await , tokio::spawn and Box::pin handle it for you; you meet Pin when storing futures in structs or writing poll by hand ( std::pin docs ).
The runtime is a library: tokio Python ships one event loop in the standard library; Node has one built in.
Rust's standard library defines the Future trait but no runtime (the executor that polls futures, plus timers and non-blocking sockets).
You add one; tokio is the de facto standard, and axum, reqwest and tonic are built on it.

Concurrency: join, spawn, JoinSet, Semaphore tokio::join!(a, b, c) polls several futures inside the current task and finishes when all are done: concurrency without new tasks. tokio::spawn(fut) hands a future to the runtime as an independent task (Python's create_task ) that may run on any worker thread, in parallel with others; it returns a JoinHandle to await the result.
A JoinSet owns a group of tasks (like asyncio.TaskGroup ) and aborts them all if it is dropped.

1. timeout(250 ms) around a 2000 ms call slow: started, waiting 2000 ms drop: slow cleaned up -> Err(Elapsed(())) after 253 ms 2. select!: first to finish wins, the other is dropped fast: started, waiting 100 ms lazy: started, waiting 300 ms fast: finished drop: fast cleaned up drop: lazy cleaned up -> winner fast after 103 ms 3. a spawned task keeps running on its own; abort() cancels it background: started, waiting 1000 ms drop: background cleaned up -> join: Err(true) 4. dropping a JoinHandle does NOT cancel the task (it is detached) detached: started, waiting 100 ms detached: finished drop: detached cleaned up -> main done Read the second case carefully: "lazy" started before "fast" because select! And the fourth: dropping a JoinHandle detaches a spawned task, it does not cancel it; only abort() (or dropping the JoinSet that owns it) does.

Python , the same timeout: cancellation is an exception raised inside the coroutine at its await, so it can run cleanup (or even catch it): 1. asyncio.timeout(0.25) around a 2000 ms call slow: started, waiting 2000 ms slow: CancelledError raised at the await finally: slow cleaned up -> TimeoutError after 252 ms What this means in practice.
In Python, cleanup goes in finally ; in Rust, cleanup goes in Drop (a guard), because there is no exception to catch.

A future that has done half its work when dropped (read part of a message, taken an item off a queue) loses that half: cancel safety . tokio documents which of its methods are cancel safe; inside select! loops, use those, or keep state outside the future.
Blocking the runtime: the mistake async makes easy A worker thread can poll only one task at a time, and it gets the thread back only at an .await .
A task that calls a blocking function ( std::thread::sleep , a synchronous file read, a CPU-heavy loop) holds its worker the whole time, and every other task queued on that worker waits.
Alice Ryhl (a tokio maintainer) gives the rule of thumb: "no more than 10 to 100 microseconds between each .await" ( Async: What is blocking? ).

Send + 'static: why tokio::spawn rejects your code A spawned task can outlive the function that spawned it ( 'static : it may not borrow its locals) and can move to another worker thread at any .await ( Send : everything it holds across an await must be safe to move between threads).
Part 1 explains Send and Sync ( Reading ); here are the three errors they produce in async code, each with the compiler's real message and the fix.

Predict, then reveal: A task that reads a local Vec without move : compiles? error[E0373]: async block may outlive the current function, but it borrows `prompts`, which is owned by the current function --> src/main.rs:5:26 | 5 | let h = tokio::spawn(async { | ^^^^^ may outlive borrowed value `prompts` 6 | println!("{} prompts", prompts.len()); | ------- `prompts` is borrowed here | = note: async blocks are not executed immediately and must either take a reference or ownership of outside variables they use help: to force the async block to take ownership of `prompts` (and any other referenced variables), use the `move` keyword | 5 | let h = tokio::spawn(async move { | ++++ For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0373`. error: could not compile `errs` (bin "errs") due to 1 previous error The fix is the one the compiler suggests: async move gives the task ownership (clone first if the caller still needs the data; for large shared data, clone an Arc ).

An HTTP service with axum The problem it solves.

Turn the token counter into something other programs call over HTTP: POST /count with {"text": "..."} returns {"tokens": n} , POST /count_log with a JSONL body returns the root program's report as JSON. axum is the tokio project's web framework: a thin, typed layer over the hyper HTTP library.
If you know FastAPI, most of it maps one to one.
HTTP design itself (methods, status codes, idempotency, versioning) is the SWE topic's page: Building a backend API .

Routes and handlers tok/src/service.rs (lines 70 to 98) pub fn app(cfg: Config) -> Router { let timeout = cfg.request_timeout; let limit = cfg.max_body_bytes; let state = Arc::new(AppState { cfg, requests: AtomicU64::new(0), tokens_counted: AtomicU64::new(0) }); Router::new() .route( "/health" , get(|| async { "ok" })) .route( "/count" , post(count)) .route( "/count_log" , post(count_log)) .route( "/slow" , get(slow)) .route( "/stats" , get(stats)) .with_state(state) // Layers wrap every route; the last added is the outermost. // axum's own extractor limit (2 MB) is replaced by one configurable limit for every route. .layer(DefaultBodyLimit::disable()) .layer(RequestBodyLimitLayer::new(limit)) .layer(TimeoutLayer::with_status_code(StatusCode::REQUEST_TIMEOUT, timeout)) .layer(TraceLayer::new_for_http()) } /// POST /count {"text": "..."} -> {"tokens": n} async fn count(State(st): State<Arc<AppState>>, Json(req): Json<CountReq>) -> Result<Json<CountResp>, AppError> { st.requests.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed); if req.text.is_empty() { return Err(AppError::Empty); } let tokens = count_tokens(&req.text); st.tokens_counted.fetch_add(tokens, Ordering::Relaxed); Ok(Json(CountResp { tokens })) } A handler is an async fn .
Its parameters are extractors : types that know how to pull something out of the request.

Json<CountReq> parses the body as JSON into the struct (serde checks every field and type, like a pydantic model); State<...> hands over shared state; Query<T> parses the query string; axum::body::Bytes takes the raw body.
Its return type must implement IntoResponse : a String , a Json<T> , a status code, a tuple of those, or a Result of two of them.
If an extractor fails, axum answers for you and the handler never runs: Predict, then reveal: Send {"txt": "oops"} (a typo in the field name).

Which status, and what body? $ curl -i -X POST localhost:3000/count -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"txt":"oops"}' HTTP/1.1 422 Unprocessable Entity content-type: text/plain; charset=utf-8 content-length: 98 date: (removed) Failed to deserialize the JSON body into the target type: missing field `text` at line 1 column 14 Predict, then reveal: Send valid JSON without a content-type: application/json header.

Which status? $ curl -i -X POST localhost:3000/count -d '{"text":"hi"}' HTTP/1.1 415 Unsupported Media Type content-type: text/plain; charset=utf-8 content-length: 54 date: (removed) Expected request with `Content-Type: application/json` Python bridge FastAPI answers the same mistake with 422 and a structured JSON detail list (recorded from the FastAPI twin in code/py/app.py : {"detail":[{"type":"missing","loc":["body","text"],"msg":"Field required",...}]} ). axum's default rejection is a plain-text sentence; to get JSON errors, write your own extractor wrapper or map rejections in a layer.
FastAPI's dependency injection corresponds to extractors and State ; Starlette middleware corresponds to tower layers.

Errors the handler returns For errors the handler decides, define an enum with thiserror (a library-style error type, so each case can map to its own status) and implement IntoResponse once: tok/src/service.rs (lines 49 to 68) /// Errors a handler can return.

IntoResponse turns each into a status code and a JSON body. #[derive(Debug, thiserror::Error)] pub enum AppError { #[error("body is not valid UTF-8")] NotUtf8, #[error("text is empty")] Empty, #[error("worker failed: {0}")] Join( #[from] tokio::task::JoinError), } impl IntoResponse for AppError { fn into_response( self ) -> Response { let status = match self { AppError::NotUtf8 | AppError::Empty => StatusCode::BAD_REQUEST, AppError::Join(_) => StatusCode::INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR, }; (status, Json(serde_json:: json!

({ "error" : self .to_string() }))).into_response() } } $ curl -i -X POST localhost:3000/count -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"text":""}' HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request content-type: application/json content-length: 25 date: (removed) {"error":"text is empty"} The #[from] tokio::task::JoinError line lets ? convert a crashed background job into a 500 automatically.

A panic (a bug such as an out-of-bounds index) inside a handler does not take the server down: tokio catches it at the task boundary, that one connection is closed without a response, and other requests carry on. examples/b3_panic.rs , with curl as the client: thread 'tokio-rt-worker' (N) panicked at examples/b3_panic.rs:25:14: index out of bounds: the len is 0 but the index is 3 note: run with `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` environment variable to display a backtrace GET /boom -> HTTP 000 (curl exit 52) GET /health -> HTTP 200 (curl exit 0) thread 'tokio-rt-worker' (N) panicked at examples/b3_panic.rs:25:14: index out of bounds: the len is 0 but the index is 3 GET /boom -> HTTP 000 (curl exit 52) GET /health -> HTTP 200 (curl exit 0) curl's exit 52 is "empty reply from server".
To answer 500 instead, add tower-http's CatchPanicLayer ; to find the bug, the panic message is on stderr with the file and line.

Shared state Every request runs as its own task, maybe on another thread, so shared state goes behind an Arc (a thread-safe shared pointer; Part 1, Reading ) and anything mutable inside it must be thread-safe: here, two atomic counters. with_state(state) gives each handler a cheap clone of the Arc .
For a mutable map, use a Mutex (held briefly, never across an await) or a concurrent map; for a database pool, the pool type is already shareable.

Python's equivalent, a module-level dict, is per worker process under uvicorn --workers 4 , so /stats on the FastAPI twin reports only the worker that answered. tokserve's counters are process-wide because its workers are threads: $ curl localhost:3000/stats {"requests":3,"tokens_counted":44703} CPU work inside a handler tok/src/service.rs (lines 100 to 113) /// POST /count_log with a JSONL body -> the root program's report as JSON. /// Counting a large body is CPU work: with offload on it runs on the blocking pool. async fn count_log(State(st): State<Arc<AppState>>, body: axum::body::Bytes) -> Result<Json< crate ::Report>, AppError> { st.requests.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed); let work = move || -> Result< crate ::Report, AppError> { let text = std::str::from_utf8(&body).map_err(|_| AppError::NotUtf8)?; let mut t = Tally::default(); t.add_text(text); Ok(t.report(5)) }; let report = if st.cfg.offload { tokio::task::spawn_blocking(work). await ?? } else { work()? }; st.tokens_counted.fetch_add(report.tokens, Ordering::Relaxed); Ok(Json(report)) } Counting a 391 KB log is about a millisecond of CPU; a 3.9 MB one about ten times that.
Either is far above the 10 to 100 µs budget between awaits, so the handler moves it to the blocking pool (the inline mode exists only for the measurement above).
Note the double ?? : the first unwraps the JoinError (did the background job panic?), the second the counting's own Result .
Middleware: tower layers A layer wraps the whole router in reusable behaviour; tower-http provides the common ones.
The last .layer added is the outermost, so a request passes through tracing, then the timeout, then the body limit, then the route.

Configuration and graceful shutdown The service reads its settings with clap, with env = "TOK_ADDR" on each flag, so the same binary takes flags on a laptop and environment variables in a container (twelve-factor style): Serve the token counter over HTTP.

Every flag can also come from the environment Usage: tokserve [OPTIONS] Options: --addr <ADDR> Address to listen on [env: TOK_ADDR=] [default: 127.0.0.1:3000] --max-body <MAX_BODY> Largest request body accepted, in bytes [env: TOK_MAX_BODY=] [default: 1048576] --timeout-ms <TIMEOUT_MS> Per-request time limit, in milliseconds [env: TOK_TIMEOUT_MS=] [default: 1000] --workers <WORKERS> Async worker threads (default: one per CPU core) [env: TOK_WORKERS=] --inline Count large bodies inline on the async worker instead of the blocking pool -h, --help Print help -V, --version Print version When an orchestrator stops a container it sends SIGTERM , waits a grace period, then sends SIGKILL: 10 s by default for docker stop ( docs ), 30 s by default on Kubernetes ( pod lifecycle ).

Deployment: a container image A container image is a file system plus a start command.
A Python service image needs an interpreter and its packages; a Rust service image needs the binary and, at most, a C library.

The standard recipe is a multi-stage build : compile in a full Rust image, then copy only the binary into a minimal one. tok/Dockerfile # Multi-stage build: compile in a full Rust image, ship only the binary. # Stage 1: the builder (about 1.5 GB of compilers and headers; thrown away).
FROM rust:1.99-slim-bookworm AS build WORKDIR /src # Cache dependencies: build once with a dummy main so code edits do not refetch crates.

COPY Cargo.toml Cargo.lock ./ RUN mkdir -p src/bin && echo 'fn main(){}' > src/bin/tokserve.rs && echo '' > src/lib.rs \ && cargo build --release --bin tokserve && rm -rf src COPY src ./src RUN touch src/lib.rs src/bin/tokserve.rs && cargo build --release --bin tokserve # Stage 2: distroless "cc" = glibc + libgcc + CA certs, no shell, no package manager, non-root user.

FROM gcr.io/distroless/cc-debian12:nonroot COPY --from=build /src/target/release/tokserve /tokserve ENV TOK_ADDR=0.0.0.0:3000 EXPOSE 3000 ENTRYPOINT [ "/tokserve" ] Two base images matter for the last stage.

Distroless images ( GoogleContainerTools/distroless ) contain no shell and no package manager, so there is less to patch and less for an attacker to use; cc-debian12 adds glibc and libgcc for a normally linked Rust binary, and the :nonroot tag runs as an unprivileged user. scratch is the empty image: it works only with a fully static binary, which the musl cross-build above produces: tok/Dockerfile.scratch # The smallest image: a static musl binary in an empty image. # Build the binary first (on any machine): see ../../cross.sh, or in a builder stage with # rustup target add x86_64-unknown-linux-musl && cargo build --release --target x86_64-unknown-linux-musl FROM scratch COPY tokserve /tokserve ENV TOK_ADDR=0.0.0.0:3000 USER 65532:65532 EXPOSE 3000 ENTRYPOINT [ "/tokserve" ] Image for this service Base (compressed, linux/arm64) + the service Source FastAPI on python:3.14-slim 47.1 MB + fastapi, pydantic, uvicorn and deps Docker Hub tag API tokserve on distroless/cc-debian12 9.0 MB + 2.84 MB binary (glibc build) gcr.io registry manifest tokserve on distroless/static-debian12 or scratch 0.7 MB / 0 + 4582976 bytes (static musl build, arm64, not stripped) gcr.io registry manifest; measured binary Not built here The Docker daemon on this laptop was not running and was not started for this page, so the two Dockerfiles are shown as written and the image sizes are base-image sizes from the registries (compressed layer sums, checked 2026-10-05) plus the binaries measured on this machine.

Common mistakes Blocking inside async code std::thread::sleep , std::fs , a synchronous HTTP client or a long CPU loop inside an async fn stalls its worker and every task queued on it.
It hides on a multi-threaded runtime until load arrives (the 300 ms line in the trace above).
Use the async API, spawn_blocking , or rayon.
Forgetting that futures are lazy Calling an async fn without .await (or spawning it) does nothing.
The compiler warns ("futures do nothing unless you .await or poll them"); do not silence the warning.
Holding a lock or a non-Send value across .await A std::sync::MutexGuard or an Rc alive at an await makes the future non- Send , and tokio::spawn refuses it.
Scope the guard so it drops before the await; use Arc ; reach for tokio::sync::Mutex only when the lock must be held across an await.
Assuming a dropped JoinHandle cancels the task It detaches it; the task keeps running.
Use abort() , or a JoinSet , which aborts its tasks when dropped.
Code that is not cancel safe inside select!
The losing branch is dropped mid-way.
If it had read half a message or popped an item, that work is lost.
Keep buffers outside the future or use methods documented as cancel safe. println! in a CLI that may be piped A closed pipe makes println! panic (exit 101).
Write through a locked stdout and treat BrokenPipe as success.
Progress and logs on stdout They corrupt the output for the next program in the pipe. stdout is for results; stderr for everything else; progress only when is_terminal() .

Benchmark and ship --release .

Decide on one limit ( DefaultBodyLimit ) and test the 413 path.
Dying on SIGTERM Without graceful shutdown every deploy drops in-flight requests.
Wire with_graceful_shutdown to SIGTERM and Ctrl-C.
